text: Vulval discharge can originate from the bladder (cystitis) or the uterus (endometritis); the disease can be prolonged and non-fatal, showing as pus in the urine or a slight discharge on the vulva/pen floor. Any vulval discharge needs treatment even if the sow looks otherwise healthy — untreated bladder infection can progress to fatal kidney infection (nephritis), and untreated uterine infection can cause infertility (pus-damaged uterus prevents embryo development); mix Tetracycline or TMP+Sulfa into feed for 1–3 weeks. Post-partum metritis specifically: abundant, foul-smelling white or brown vulval discharge starting 4–5 days after delivery, fever over 40°C, poor/no appetite, often combined with mastitis signs (hard udder) and agalactia (no milk). Treatment: inject TMP+Sulfa, Enrofloxacin, Amoxicillin, or OTC for 3 days, plus a single Prostaglandin dose to clear infectious material from the uterus. Prevention: inject all sows with 2 ml Oxytocin at the end of delivery to ensure the whole placenta is expelled.
